lesson.title: Describing Matter Without Changing It: Physical Properties
lesson.summary: This section defines physical properties, distinguishes intensive from extensive properties, and works through a density calculation used to identify a substance.
lesson.body:
Every sample of matter, whether an element, compound, or mixture, has a set of physical properties: characteristics that can be observed or measured without changing what the substance actually is at the chemical level. Color, odor, density, hardness, melting point, boiling point, and solubility are all physical properties. You can measure the density of a gold ring, note its shiny yellow color, and record that it melts at 1064 degrees Celsius, all without breaking a single chemical bond or turning the gold into anything else. After every one of those measurements, the substance in front of you is still gold. This is what separates a physical property from a chemical property, covered in the next section, where identifying the property necessarily destroys or transforms the original substance.

Physical properties are also divided into two important categories: intensive and extensive. An intensive property does not depend on how much of the substance you have; density, melting point, boiling point, and color stay the same whether you have a gram of the substance or a kilogram. An extensive property does depend on the amount present; mass, volume, and total length are all extensive, since a bigger sample simply has more mass and more volume. This distinction matters because intensive properties are useful for identifying a substance, a chemist can confirm an unknown liquid is ethanol by checking that it boils at 78.4 degrees Celsius, regardless of how much liquid is in the flask, while extensive properties tell you nothing about identity on their own, since a large sample of water and a small sample of water share nothing in their mass or volume alone.

Density is one of the most useful intensive physical properties in chemistry precisely because it lets you identify a substance from a small sample. Density is defined as mass divided by volume, usually expressed in grams per cubic centimeter for solids and liquids. Pure gold has a density of 19.3 grams per cubic centimeter, far higher than nearly any other common metal, which is exactly why gold prospectors historically used a pan and water to separate heavy gold flecks from lighter surrounding rock and sand. As a worked example, suppose you measure an unknown metal block with a mass of 54.0 grams and, using water displacement, find it occupies a volume of 20.0 cubic centimeters. Dividing mass by volume gives 54.0 grams divided by 20.0 cubic centimeters, which equals 2.7 grams per cubic centimeter, a value that matches the known density of aluminum, letting you identify the metal without running any chemical test at all.

Because physical properties can be measured without altering a substance's chemical identity, they are the first tool chemists reach for when trying to identify an unknown material or verify the purity of a known one. A single measured property rarely proves identity on its own, since more than one substance can share a density or a color, but combining several physical properties, density alongside melting point alongside solubility behavior, narrows the possibilities quickly and reliably. Physical properties also set up the next section's topic directly: a physical change is any transformation, like melting, freezing, or dissolving, that alters one or more of these physical properties while leaving the substance's fundamental chemical composition untouched.
